claims.text: Composition-induced lattice distortion is the primary driver of enhanced high-temperature yield strength in refractory high-entropy alloys.
Composition-induced lattice distortion alters the thermoelastic behavior of refractory high-entropy alloys.
A standard NbTaTiV-type refractory alloy has high naturally occurring lattice distortion in its as-fabricated state.
Tailoring elemental proportions can produce a baseline alloy with reduced lattice distortion.
Testing near 900°C in an inert atmosphere under controlled strain rates and thermal cycles minimizes oxidation and environmental effects.
Atomic-scale lattice distortions affect dislocation core structures and solute-dislocation interaction energies.
Greater lattice distortion intensifies dislocation-solute interactions and promotes dislocation pinning.
The intensified dislocation-solute interaction caused by lattice distortion raises high-temperature yield strength.
Increased lattice distortion modifies the elastic moduli of refractory high-entropy alloys.
Reducing lattice distortion will alter both the elastic and plastic deformation response.
The high-distortion alloy will retain significantly greater yield strength at high temperature than the reduced-distortion baseline.
The high-distortion alloy will have different elastic moduli from the reduced-distortion baseline.
The high-distortion alloy will exhibit more compact dislocation cores than the reduced-distortion baseline.
The reduced-distortion baseline will have reduced elastic anisotropy relative to the high-distortion alloy.
Dislocation slip controls elevated-temperature plastic deformation in at least one refractory multi-principal-element alloy.
Secondary microstructural factors or minor phase instabilities may influence measured yield strength and elastic moduli.
Failure to observe statistically significant strength, modulus, or dislocation-characteristic differences between the two alloys would falsify the proposed dominant role of lattice distortion.
